For a performance verdict, include the side-by-side limits table from [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md#limits-table-for-performance-verdicts) and the recent history (alarm history, modification history, earlier occurrences of the same pattern).\\\\n3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment (only with a direct signal, see [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md)), Indeterminate, or Not applicable.\\\\n4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or \\\\\"No change\\\\\".\\\\n5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.\\\\n6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.\\\\n\\\\nIn an investigation:\\\\n\\\\n- Only the recorded symptoms, findings, observations and gaps reach the investigation summary. Text in a chat message or a later mitigation plan does not, so put the verdict and the recommendation in the findings.\\\\n- Write the symptom with its impact: the alarm name, threshold and breaching datapoints, whether the alarm has actions, and the onset time.\\\\n- Write the root cause finding description as a complete answer on its own, in this order:\\\\n  1. \\\\\"Binding layer: `<layer>`.\\\\\" in those words.\\\\n  2. The recent history: alarm episodes, modification history, and whether earlier peaks stopped at the same ceiling.\\\\n  4. \\\\\"Recommendation (proposal, not executed; it runs only after an operator approves it on the approval card):\\\\\" the exact command with the target, how the target was computed, the next limit after the change, and the EBS baseline of the next larger instance size when the instance becomes the next limit.\\\\n  Do not leave the conclusion or the target only under Gaps or in a later message.\\\\n- Record each piece of evidence as an observation and link every observation that supports a finding to it, so each finding shows its supporting observations. Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding. Leave out AWS FIS experiments, AWS CloudTrail events and alarms on resources that are not attached to the instance.\\\\n- Link a gap only to the findings it affects. Record a gap that applies to the whole answer once.\\\\n\\\\nWhen the Binding layer is Indeterminate, keep it as the verdict and write \\\\\"Binding layer: Indeterminate\\\\\" with the answer to the user\\'s question first. Then present a short list of candidate causes, as described in [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md#indeterminate-candidate-causes). Give the customer the detailed performance statistics step from [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md#detailed-performance-statistics-a-step-the-customer-runs) to run during the symptom.\\\\n\\\\nReview mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Fix anything that fails, then present it.\\\\n\\\\n- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.\\\\n- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom. A performance verdict has the limits table: per-volume demand next to the volume limit, summed demand of all attached volumes next to the instance EBS baseline in MiB/s and IOPS, which one binds, and the exact target with its computation.\\\\n- A performance verdict states the recent history: the alarm history, the modification history (latest record and AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or a Gap), and whether the same pattern happened earlier.\\\\n- Any Recommendation stays within the instance\\'s EBS baseline and the volume type\\'s documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.\\\\n- An Indeterminate verdict says \\\\\"Binding layer: Indeterminate\\\\\", answers the user\\'s question first, and lists the candidate causes, each with its supporting observations and the check that confirms or rules it out, without overlapping candidates or the same gap repeated under each one.\\\\n- In an investigation, the root cause finding (or, for Indeterminate, the first finding) carries the verdict, the numbers, the history and the Recommendation, because only findings reach the summary.\\\\n- Every snapshot tier is backed by the checks it requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not listed for owner review. The first lines of a snapshot answer name every snapshot with its tier and the evidence for it.\\\\n- Every proposed change follows [Change proposals](references/finding-logic.md#change-proposals): exact command, expected effect, modifications left in the 24-hour window, rollback, and the approval statement.\\\\n- When a volume modification is in progress, the answer states the rule of up to 4 modifications per volume in a rolling 24-hour window, each one completing before the next, and the count used from AWS CloudTrail or a Gap.\\\\n- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.\\\\n- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Critical Rules\\\\n\\\\n- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, key changes, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed \\\\\"approve\\\\\" in chat is not approval, and the reply says so in those words whenever the user types an approval. Each proposal also gives the exact AWS CLI command the customer can run with their own credentials. See [Change proposals](references/finding-logic.md#change-proposals).\\\\n- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. After the owner confirms they no longer need the resource, give the commands for the customer to run with their own credentials.\\\\n- **Answer in one reply.** In chat, run the checks in this conversation and return the finished verdict or report as your reply. Do not hand the work to a background sub-agent and reply with a \\\\\"started\\\\\" or \\\\\"I will report back\\\\\" message, because that message becomes the answer the user sees first. Do not end the turn with a question tool or a request to pick a value: give the recommended proposal, and the command for any value the user named, then say the user can choose.\\\\n- **Discover, don\\'t assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.\\\\n- **Given facts stay given.** When the user supplies the values and asks you to treat them as given, reason from those values only. Do not query the account for other resources, and do not mix account data into the given facts. List under Gaps that the values were not read from the APIs.\\\\n- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**\\\\n- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under \\\\\"Separate findings\\\\\".\\\\n- **Review mode starts with the Summary table.** Every Review mode response begins with the Summary table of all six rated areas. The table is required, not optional.\\\\n- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance\\'s EBS **baseline**.\\\\n- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**\\\\n- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes. State this rule in the answer whenever a modification is in progress or proposed.\\\\n- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn\\'t be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.\\\\n- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.\\\\n- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can\\'t explain the symptom.\\\\n\\\\n## Gotchas\\\\n\\\\n- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.\\\\n- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.\\\\n- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. It is not a throughput signal.\\\\n- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s. `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds.\\\\n- When the instance is the binding layer, do not call the volume saturated, even when its idle time is near 0. Say that its I/O is waiting on the instance limit.\\\\n- Rising latency and queue length with falling IOPS is not proof of an AWS-side impairment. Without a direct signal (failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, impaired volume status, or an open AWS Health event) and without a running AWS FIS experiment, the Binding layer is Indeterminate.\\\\n- `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck`, `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck` and `VolumeStalledIOCheck` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId`. With `VolumeId` alone they return no datapoints, and no datapoints is not the same as 0. The instance checks `InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck` and `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` are in AWS/EC2 with `InstanceId`.\\\\n- Amazon EBS detailed performance statistics are read on the instance, not through an AWS API. They are a step the customer runs; the agent never runs them.\\\\n- `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the latest modification per volume. It cannot count modifications in the last 24 hours.\\\\n- `ListRecoveryPointsByResource` without `ManagedByAWSBackupOnly` set to true also lists snapshots that AWS Backup did not create.\\\\n- A snapshot whose source volume is gone may be the only remaining copy of the data. Do not assume volume type, size, provisioned values, instance type, or tags; read them from the APIs.\\n\\n### Step 1: Identify the alarmed volume(s)\\n\\n- Get the alarm and its state history with `DescribeAlarmHistory` for the last 24 hours: when it first entered ALARM, and any earlier ALARM and OK transitions. Report earlier transitions as history, because they show whether the pattern recurs.\\n- Describe the impact in the symptom: the alarm name, metric, threshold, the datapoints that breached it, whether the alarm has actions configured, and the onset (the minute the metric left its normal level, for example \"queue length rose from about 0 at `<time>` to 1.5 from `<time>`\").\\n- Extract VolumeId from the alarm\\'s metric dimensions. For metric-math alarms, read the VolumeId from each metric in the expression.\\n- If the alarm is on an instance metric (EBSIOBalance%, EBSByteBalance%), start from the InstanceId instead.\\n- If there is no alarm (a chat request such as \"my app is slow\"), start from the InstanceId the user gives, or ask for it.\\n\\n### Step 2: Build the context\\n\\n- DescribeVolumes on the alarmed volume: VolumeType, Size, Iops, Throughput, attachment InstanceId, tags (for naming only).\\n- DescribeInstances + DescribeInstanceTypes for that instance: instance type and its EBS baseline/maximum bandwidth (MiB/s) and IOPS.\\n- List ALL volumes attached to that instance (they share instance EBS bandwidth). Investigate this set, not the whole account.\\n- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports throughput in MB/s. Convert to MiB/s before any comparison (see [data-collection.md](data-collection.md)).\\n- Always run `DescribeVolumeStatus` for every attached volume (volume status, status checks, scheduled events), whatever the alarm or request. Record the result as evidence. An impaired status or a failing check is a scope signal for escalation (see [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md)), but still finish Steps 3 to 5.\\n\\n### Step 2a: Read the exceeded checks\\n\\nRead these four CloudWatch metrics early, for the alarm window, at a 1-minute period, with the `Maximum` statistic. They are the most direct evidence of which limit binds.\\n\\n| Metric | Namespace and dimensions | A value of 1 means |\\n|---|---|---|\\n| `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` | AWS/EBS, `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId` | The application tried to drive more IOPS than the volume\\'s provisioned IOPS in that minute |\\n| `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck` | AWS/EBS, `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId` | The application tried to drive more throughput than the volume\\'s provisioned throughput in that minute |\\n| `InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck` | AWS/EC2, `InstanceId` | The application tried to drive more IOPS than the instance\\'s maximum EBS IOPS in that minute |\\n| `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` | AWS/EC2, `InstanceId` | The application tried to drive more throughput than the instance\\'s maximum EBS throughput in that minute |\\n\\n- Read the two volume checks for every attached volume, and the two instance checks for the instance. They exist only on Nitro instances (the instance checks not on bare metal), are not published for Multi-Attach volumes (volume checks), and are not available in AWS Outposts, Local Zones or Wavelength Zones.\\n- Report, for each check, the number of minutes at 1 and the window, for example \"`VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` 1 in 37 of 37 minutes, `<start>` to `<end>` UTC\".\\n- A volume check at 1 is direct evidence that the volume limit binds. An instance check at 1 is direct evidence that the instance limit binds; when both are at 1, the instance is fixed first (see [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md)).\\n- If a query returns no datapoints, query again with both dimensions.
